system.doc:
`os.system(command)` - run a shell command and collect its output.

The command runs through a shell, which is how an argument becomes a command, so this
needs `--allow-process`. It no longer blocks the interpreter while the command runs:
the task parks and every other task keeps going.

`process.run(command, args)` is the safer choice when the arguments are not fixed text,
because it does not involve a shell at all.

systemInfo.doc: the common ones in one object

v1.doc: time-based, so values sort roughly by creation

compress.doc: keep where a flag is true

filter.doc: `iter.filter(items, fn)`: only the values `fn` accepts, lazily.

take.doc: `iter.take(items, n)`: the first `n` values. Stops asking once it has them, so `count()` can feed it.

skip.doc: `iter.skip(items, n)`: everything after the first `n` values.

toArray.doc: `iter.toArray(items)`: every value, in an array. Never give it something endless.

forEach.doc: `iter.forEach(items, fn)`: call `fn` with every value, in order; `fn` may suspend.

symbol.doc: the protocol symbol a custom iterable implements

iter.doc:
`iter`: lazy sequences.

Like every library in the language, `iter` is a set of functions that take what they
work on as their first argument - `iter.take(iter.count(), 3)`, `iter.map(items, fn)` -
never methods chained on a value. The only member an iterator has is `next()`.

Every iterator this library hands out is built in one place (`makeIterator`) around a
single source of steps (a `Pull`). `it.next()`, `for (x in it)` and every function here
read from that same source, so mixing them is safe: `next()` followed by `for (x in it)`
continues where `next` stopped instead of starting over, and an iterator that is
finished stays finished.

A step may suspend. A callback given to `map` or `filter` may wait, sleep or use a
channel, and a value that implements `symbol.iterator` in the language - an object with
`[symbol.iterator]`, or a struct that declares `func [symbol.iterator]()` - is accepted
anywhere an iterable is, with its `next` called as the language function it is.

Map.doc: keys of any type, in insertion order

Counter.doc: counts how often each value appears

DefaultDict.doc: a map that fills in a missing key

listen.doc:
`server.listen(port, host, callback)` - bind the port and start accepting.

This parks until the port is actually bound, and reports a failure as an error the
program can catch. It used to return at once and print a failed bind to the
console: the program then carried on believing it had a server, and the only sign
was an exit code at the very end. It also returns where it ended up listening,
which is the only way to learn the port when binding to port 0.

fs.doc:
`fs` - the file system.

Every operation is non-blocking. The direct form parks the calling task on the host's
asynchronous file API and lets every other task keep running, so `spawn fs.readFile(...)`
really is concurrent - which is exactly what the old synchronous implementation could
not do, however it was spawned. The callback form is kept for programs that prefer it.

Permissions: reading checks `--allow-read`, writing checks `--allow-write`, and an
operation that does both (`rename`, `copyFile`, `move`) checks both, on both paths.

Binary data in and out of this library is always the language's `bytes` value, produced
by the shared kernel (`library/kernel/buffers`), so what `fs.readFile` returns can be
handed straight to `bytes`, `crypto`, `compress`, `archive`, `tcp` or `ws`.

TransformStream.doc: a stream you feed and read

EventBus.doc: a shared emitter with namespaced topics

Spawn.doc: runtime.Spawn(callback): a task that is created now and started later with `.run()`.

schedule.doc: queue a task to run after the current one yields

scheduleFirst.doc: queue it ahead of the others

waitForIdle.doc: park until every queued task has run

Sleep.doc: Suspends only the calling task; every other task keeps running.

Throttle.doc: run `fn` at most once per interval

typeOf.doc: the language's own type name for a value

hashFile.doc:
Hashing a file reads it, so it needs `--allow-read` exactly like `fs.readFile`, and it
reads without blocking: a large file no longer stops every other task.

base64Encode.doc: base64 text from binary or text

hexEncode.doc: hex text from binary or text

aesEncrypt.doc: AES with a key you supply

aesDecrypt.doc: AES with a key you supply

beforeEach.doc: register a hook; the hook itself may suspend

afterEach.doc: register a hook; the hook itself may suspend

deepEq.doc: the formatter and comparison the assertions use

bytes.doc: `bytes(n)` - the next `n` bytes, or the rest when `n` is omitted.

string.doc: `string(n, encoding)` - `n` bytes decoded as text ("utf8" by default).

varint.doc: LEB128 unsigned varint, as used by many container formats.

seek.doc: Move the cursor to an absolute position.

skip.doc: Move the cursor by a relative amount.

reader.doc:
`binary.reader(source, endian)` - a cursor over binary data.
Every read advances the cursor and fails loudly past the end, so a truncated message is
reported where it happens instead of silently producing zeros.

writer.doc:
`binary.writer(endian)` - builds binary data.
Every write returns the writer, so calls chain; `build()` produces the `bytes` value.

concat.doc: `binary.concat([a, b, ...])` - join binary chunks into one `bytes`.

check.doc: `validation.check(schema, value)` - `{ valid, value, errors }`, never throws.

parse.doc: `validation.parse(schema, value)` - the validated value, or a thrown error.

isSchema.doc: `validation.isSchema(value)` - was this produced by this library?

gzip.doc: pack with gzip (a zlib stream plus a gzip header)

deflateRaw.doc: Raw deflate: no zlib header, as ZIP entries and some protocols use.

decompress.doc: `compress.decompress(data)` - unpack gzip or zlib data without being told which.

ratio.doc: `compress.ratio(original, packed)` - how much smaller it got, as a fraction.

write.doc: Feed a chunk in; parks until the transform has taken it.

read.doc: Whatever the transform has produced so far, as `bytes`.

finish.doc:
No more input: flush the transform and return everything still unread.
The stream is finished afterwards, but `close()` is still safe to call.

buffered.doc: How many bytes of output are waiting to be read.

close.doc: Releases the resource. Safe to call twice; `defer` calls it automatically.

closed.doc: `true` once the resource has been released.

file.doc:
`compress.file(kind, source, destination)` - convert a file without holding it.

The whole-buffer functions need the input *and* the output in memory at once, which a
multi-gigabyte file cannot satisfy and `--max-memory` should not allow. This reads,
transforms and writes in chunks, so the memory it uses does not depend on the size of
the file. Returns the number of bytes written.

compress.doc:
`compress` - gzip, deflate, brotli and raw deflate over `bytes`.

    var packed = compress.gzip(data);
    var back   = compress.gunzip(packed);

Compression is CPU work that the host runs on its thread pool, so every function here
parks the calling task instead of blocking: other tasks keep running while a large
buffer is packed, and `spawn compress.gzip(...)` is genuinely concurrent.

Input and output are always the shared `bytes` value (`library/kernel/buffers`), so what
comes out of `fs.readFile` goes straight in, and what comes out goes straight to
`fs.writeFile`, `archive`, `tcp` or `ws` without conversion.

read.doc:
`archive.read(data)` - entries of a zip, tar or gzipped tar, without being told which.
This is the function most programs want: it recognises the format and unpacks it.

extract.doc:
`archive.extract(data, destination)` - unpack an archive onto disk.

Needs `--allow-write` for the destination. Entry names that would escape it are
rejected rather than written, so an untrusted archive cannot reach outside.

extractFile.doc:
`archive.extractFile(archivePath, destination)` - unpack an archive from disk.

`archive.extract` needs the whole archive in memory as a `bytes` value first, which a
multi-gigabyte archive cannot satisfy. This reads it from disk instead: a tar is walked
block by block, and a zip through its directory, one entry at a time. The memory it
uses depends on the largest entry, not on the size of the archive.

Needs `--allow-read` for the archive and `--allow-write` for the destination. Entry
names are checked the same way as in `archive.extract`, so an untrusted archive cannot
write outside the destination.

create.doc:
`archive.create(sourceDir, format)` - pack a directory into a zip or tar.
Needs `--allow-read` for the directory.

createFile.doc:
`archive.createFile(sourceDir, archivePath, format)` - pack a directory onto disk.

`archive.create` builds the whole archive as one value, so packing a large tree needs
room for the tree and the archive at once. This writes the archive as it goes: each
file is streamed from disk into the output, so what the program holds does not depend
on the size of the tree or of any file in it.

Needs `--allow-read` for the directory and `--allow-write` for the archive.

archive.doc:
`archive` - reading and writing tar and zip archives.

    var files = archive.read(fs.readFile("bundle.zip"));   // entries, as bytes
    var data  = archive.zip([{ name: "a.txt", data: "hello" }]);
    archive.extract(data, "./out");                        // writes to disk

The archive itself is a `bytes` value, so it can come from `fs`, from an HTTP response,
or from a socket without being written to disk first. Compression is not reimplemented
here: deflate comes from `compress` and gzip wrapping from `compress.gzip`, exactly as a
program would call them. Writing to disk goes through the same permission checks as
`fs`, because it is the same operation.

lookup.doc:
`dns.lookup(hostname, family)` - the address the operating system would use.

This is what a connection does, so it honours `/etc/hosts` and the system resolver,
unlike `dns.resolve`, which always queries a DNS server.

lookupAll.doc: `dns.lookupAll(hostname)` - every address the system resolver knows for a name.

resolve.doc: `dns.resolve(hostname, type)` - query a DNS server directly.

reverse.doc: `dns.reverse(address)` - the names that point at an address.

servers.doc: `dns.servers()` - the resolvers currently in use. Needs `--allow-sys`.

isIP.doc: `dns.isIP(text)` - 4, 6, or 0 when it is not an address at all.

dns.doc:
`dns` - name resolution.

    var address = dns.lookup("example.com");
    var records = dns.resolve("example.com", "MX");

Every lookup parks the calling task on the host resolver, so a slow or unreachable DNS
server delays only the task that asked, never the whole program.

Permissions: resolving a name is a network operation, so it needs `--allow-net`. A grant
naming hosts (`--allow-net=api.example.com`) allows resolving exactly those names; a
bare `--allow-net` allows any.

setKeepAlive.doc:
`socket.setKeepAlive(enabled, delay)` - ask the system to probe an idle peer.

A peer that disappears without closing - a cable pulled, a machine that lost
power - leaves a socket that looks open and never produces anything. Keep-alive
probes make the system notice and fail the socket instead of waiting forever.
`delay` is how long the socket may be idle, in milliseconds, before the first
probe; it defaults to the system's own setting.

connectUnix.doc:
`tcp.connectUnix(path, options)` - connect to a unix domain socket.

A unix socket is a file rather than a host and port: there is no network involved, and
two processes on one machine talk through the filesystem. That is what most database
servers and service managers offer locally, and it is faster than a loopback
connection because nothing is routed.

It is a file, so it needs `--allow-read` for the path rather than `--allow-net`.
Everything the returned socket can do is what `tcp.connect` returns.

listenUnix.doc:
`tcp.listenUnix(path, options)` - serve on a unix domain socket.

The path is created when the server binds. A path left behind by a process that did not
shut down cleanly would make binding fail, so `{ force: true }` removes a stale one
first; without it an existing path is an error, which is the safer default - it stops
one server from quietly taking another's socket.

Needs `--allow-write` for the path, since binding creates a file there. Closing the
server removes it.

isPortFree.doc: `tcp.isPortFree(port, host)` - can something bind here right now?

receive.doc:
`receive()` - the next datagram as `{ data, address, port }`, parking until one
arrives. `receive(timeoutMs)` gives up after the timeout and returns `nil`.

pending.doc: How many datagrams have arrived and are not taken yet.

setBroadcast.doc: Allow sending to the broadcast address.

open.doc:
`udp.open(port, options)` - bind a datagram socket.

`port` 0 picks a free one; `options.type` is "udp4" (default) or "udp6", and
`options.reuseAddr` lets several sockets share the port.

udp.doc:
`udp` - datagram sockets.

    var sock = defer udp.open(0);          // any free port
    sock.send("ping", "127.0.0.1", 9000);
    var packet = sock.receive();           // { data, address, port }

A socket is an owned resource: `symbol.dispose` closes it, so `defer` releases it at the
end of the block, `close()` is idempotent, and every operation is a coroutine, so
`spawn` / `wait` work and a socket waiting for a datagram never blocks other tasks.

Incoming datagrams are queued as they arrive, because the host delivers them whenever it
likes rather than when the program asks; `receive()` takes from that queue or parks for
the next one.

Permissions: opening a socket and sending both need `--allow-net`, which may name hosts
and ports.

listen.doc:
`ws.listen(port, host, options)` - accept WebSocket connections.

`accept()` returns the next connection; `accept(handler)` runs `handler(peer)` for each
one as its own task, so several clients are served at the same time.

Giving `options.cert` and `options.key` makes it a `wss://` server: the same protocol
over TLS, so clients connect with `wss://` and nothing else about it changes.

post.doc:
`post(value, options)` - send a value to the worker.

Plain data and `bytes` both cross. By default the bytes are copied, so the
value stays usable here; `post(value, { transfer: true })` hands the memory
over instead, which costs nothing for a large buffer but leaves this side's
copy empty. Use it when the value is being given away, not shared.

receive.doc:
`receive()` - the next value the worker posted, parking until there is one.
Returns `nil` once the worker has finished and sent nothing more.

result.doc: `result()` - park until the worker's program finishes, then its value.

close.doc: Releases the resource. Safe to call twice; `defer` calls it automatically.

closed.doc: `true` once the resource has been released.

start.doc:
`workers.start(file, options)` - run a MyLang file on another thread.

`options.data` is handed to the worker as `worker.data`; it is copied, not shared, so
the two sides never see each other's objects.

run.doc:
`run(value, options)` - give one job to a free thread and park for its answer.

`options` is passed to the thread the same way `post` takes it, so
`{ transfer: true }` hands binary over instead of copying it.

busy.doc: `busy()` - how many threads are working right now.

queued.doc: `queued()` - how many jobs are waiting for a free thread.

close.doc: Releases the resource. Safe to call twice; `defer` calls it automatically.

closed.doc: `true` once the resource has been released.

pool.doc:
`workers.pool(file, size, options)` - a fixed set of threads sharing a queue of work.

    var pool = defer workers.pool("./hash.ml", 4);
    var tasks = [];
    for (var file in files) { tasks[length(tasks)] = spawn pool.run(file) }
    var hashes = wait.all(tasks);

`start` gives one thread per call, which is the wrong shape for many small jobs: a
thread costs several milliseconds to create and a few megabytes to keep, so starting
one per item spends more than the work. A pool creates its threads once and hands each
one job at a time, so the cost is paid once however many jobs follow.

The worker file is written as a loop over `worker.receive()`: for every value it
receives it posts one answer back. `run(value)` sends a value, parks until the answer
comes, and returns it - so from the caller's side it reads like an ordinary call, and
several of them in `spawn` tasks fill the pool without any of them blocking the others.

Needs `--allow-worker`, like `start`, and counts against `--max-workers` once per
thread. `close()` - which `defer` calls - ends every thread.

cpus.doc: `workers.cpus()` - how many threads the machine can usefully run. Needs `--allow-sys`.

workers.doc:
`workers` - running MyLang code on another thread.

    var w = defer workers.start("./heavy.ml", { data: 1000000 });
    w.post("go");
    coreio.print(w.receive());
    coreio.print(w.result());

The interpreter is single-threaded by design: `spawn` gives concurrency, not
parallelism, so one task that computes for a long time holds the thread. A worker is the
answer to exactly that case - the file runs on its own thread, with its own interpreter,
and the two sides exchange messages.

Inside the worker file, a `worker` object is available without importing anything:

    worker.data              what `start` passed in
    worker.post(value)       send a value back
    worker.receive()         take the next value sent to this worker (parks)

A worker is an owned resource: `symbol.dispose` terminates it, so `defer` guarantees the
thread is not left running when the block exits. Every operation parks instead of
blocking, so waiting for a worker never stops the other tasks.

Permissions: starting a worker needs `--allow-worker`, and the worker inherits the
parent's whole policy - a sandboxed program cannot widen its permissions by starting a
thread.

run.doc: `process.run(command, args, options)` - run to completion and collect the output.

pipeline.doc:
`process.pipeline(stages, options)` - run several programs with the output of each
feeding the next.

    var out = process.pipeline([
      ["git", ["log", "--format=%an"]],
      ["sort"],
      ["uniq", ["-c"]],
      ["sort", ["-rn"]]
    ]);
    coreio.print(out.stdout.toString());

This is the shell's `a | b | c`, and it is what a shell is usually wanted for. Building
it by hand means reading each program's output into memory and writing it to the next,
which holds the whole stream at every stage; here each stage's output goes straight into
the next one's input, so a large stream passes through without being collected.

Every stage is checked against `--allow-process` separately, so a grant naming commands
(`--allow-process=git,sort`) covers a pipeline only if it names all of them.

Returns `{code, stdout, stderr, stages}`: the exit code of the *last* stage, its output,
the errors from every stage together, and a per-stage list of codes - a pipeline where
an early stage failed still produces output, so the codes are worth seeing.

`wait` is needed: the task parks until the last program exits.

setKeepAlive.doc:
`socket.setKeepAlive(enabled, delay)` - ask the system to probe an idle peer.

A peer that disappears without closing - a cable pulled, a machine that lost
power - leaves a socket that looks open and never produces anything. Keep-alive
probes make the system notice and fail the socket instead of waiting forever.
`delay` is how long the socket may be idle, in milliseconds, before the first
probe; it defaults to the system's own setting.

listen.doc:
`tls.listen(port, host, options)` - accept encrypted connections.

`options.cert` and `options.key` are required: a TLS server has nothing to present
without them. Both may be inline material or `{ file: "path" }`.

rootCertificates.doc: `tls.rootCertificates()` - the certificate authorities the host trusts.

tls.doc:
`tls` - encrypted TCP.

    var socket = defer tls.connect("example.com", 443);
    socket.write("GET / HTTP/1.0\r\nHost: example.com\r\n\r\n");
    coreio.print(socket.readAll().toString());

A TLS socket is a `tcp` socket that happens to be encrypted: reading, writing,
buffering, `close()` and `symbol.dispose` are literally the same code (see
`library/net/socket`), so anything written against `tcp` works here unchanged. Only
establishing the connection differs, and that is what this library adds.

Certificates are verified by default. Turning that off (`rejectUnauthorized: false`)
makes the encryption decorative - anyone in the middle can read and change everything -
so it exists for a self-signed certificate during development and nothing else.

Permissions: `connect` and `listen` need `--allow-net`, exactly as in `tcp`; reading a
certificate or key from a file needs `--allow-read`.
